connections.feedback: Oversight works best when it matches risk: full review where harm is likely, sampling elsewhere, and error tracking to improve over time.
Reviewing everything equally is safe and may be right for a small team, but it can lead to tired, shallow reviews. Many experts prefer a tiered approach.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: safe but can cause the review fatigue that weakens the check.

connections.feedback: Past performance does not remove the need for oversight where the stakes are high.
A short reply can still cause harm, and customers should not have to correct mistakes.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Reminders rarely fix a habit that comes from how the work is set up. Change the process so attention is rewarded and measured.
Clearer written steps may help a bit, but they do not address why reviewers have stopped reading closely.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: addresses process but not the cause.

connections.feedback: A second AI step can share the first one's blind spots and removes the human check.
People trust fluent output over time. Seeded errors and rotation make attention measurable and keep it up.

connections.feedback: Length is not the main danger. What matters is whether the summary keeps the facts the next step depends on.
Speed is usually the benefit of automation, not the risk. The danger lies in errors passing unseen from one step to the next.
In a chain, each step trusts the last. A small distortion can grow, and by the end nobody sees where it started.
Cost may matter, but the central danger is that errors compound unseen from one step to the next. Add a check between the steps.

connections.feedback: Time saved is a real reason to automate, and long tasks have the most to gain. But it does not tell you how risky a mistake would be.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: a real factor but not the one that should weigh most.

connections.feedback: Start where a mistake is cheap and easy to undo. Move toward higher-stakes work only as checks and confidence grow.
How new a tool is says nothing about whether a task suits it. Weigh how serious and reversible a mistake would be instead.
Enjoyment is not a sound basis for deciding where AI is safe. Weigh how serious and reversible a mistake would be instead.

connections.feedback: Popularity is not evidence of accuracy for your use. Ask what the claim was measured on and whether that matches your work.
A polished demo usually shows the best case, not typical results. Ask what it was measured on and test it on your own examples.
A measured accuracy only applies to the kind of work it was measured on. Ask whether that matches yours, then test on your own examples.
A higher number only matters if it was measured on comparable material in a comparable way.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Some rules are needed before anyone starts, such as what data may not be entered. But detailed rules written without experience tend to miss real problems.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: some upfront rules are essential; detailed ones are premature.

connections.feedback: Real experience on low-risk tasks produces habits grounded in what actually happens, and spreading gradually builds trust.
Forcing broad use before habits exist spreads mistakes quickly. Start small, learn what works, and then widen use.
People repeat the same avoidable errors when nothing is shared. Gather what works and what fails, and turn it into simple team habits.

connections.feedback: Reuse is valuable, and templates do the job without the client data. Sensitive details stay out of anything widely shared.
Being trusted does not make wide sharing of client data appropriate. Fewer people should hold it.
Reviewing outputs is good practice, but it does not address client data stored in the library itself. Keep real data out of what is shared.
A shared library of clean templates is a good practice. The risk is the data in it, not the sharing.

connections.feedback: Abandoning it is an overreaction, because the routine may work fine on the new input. Test it first and decide from the results.
Sampling outputs is a fair ongoing check, but when the input type changes you want a deliberate test on the new material, not just routine sampling.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: good in general, but weaker than a targeted retest.

connections.feedback: Months of success do not cover new kinds of input. Test the routine on the new documents before relying on it.
A routine that worked on one kind of input is not proven on another. Test it again whenever the input changes.

connections.feedback: Full review is the safest and may suit small volumes. At scale it tends to become shallow, so most experts prefer a risk-based approach.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: safe but can lose effectiveness at volume.

connections.feedback: A tool cannot provide independent oversight of its own output, because it can repeat its own errors. Oversight needs a person.
Skipping review leaves errors for customers and colleagues to find. Review where harm is likely and sample the rest.
Match oversight to risk and track the errors you find, so the checking improves over time.

connections.feedback: Months of success do not cover new kinds of input.
A routine proven on one kind of input is not proven on another. Test it on the new material and compare with earlier results.
A tool cannot reliably judge its own performance on new material, and it may simply say yes. Test it with samples you can check.
Sampling is a fair ongoing check, but when the input type changes you want a deliberate test on the new material.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: good in general, but weaker than a targeted retest.

connections.feedback: Even low-stakes replies can contain mistakes or an unhelpful tone. At this volume, reading them is cheap.
A tool cannot give independent review of its own output. At this volume, a person can read everything.
A risk-based plan also works and scales if volume grows. For ten low-stakes replies a week, though, it adds more process than the situation needs.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: sound in general; heavier than needed at this size.

connections.feedback: At this volume and risk, reading every reply is cheap and leaves no gaps. Tiered systems are for larger volumes.
